passage:
When the internet arrived, a good many people predicted that public libraries would close. If any fact could be looked up from home, what was the building for?

The prediction was wrong, but not because borrowing held up. In most countries the number of books lent each year has indeed fallen. What rose instead was the number of visits. People came, and kept coming, for reasons that had little to do with the shelves.

Surveys in several cities found the same pattern. The service users named most often was free internet access, used mainly by those without a connection at home — job seekers filling in applications, older residents managing pensions, new arrivals dealing with paperwork in an unfamiliar language. After that came a request that surprised the researchers: somewhere warm, quiet and free to sit, where nobody expects you to buy anything.

Libraries have adapted accordingly. Many now run language classes, homework clubs and sessions teaching people to use a smartphone. Some lend tools, musical instruments or seeds. A few employ social workers, having found that the people who most need help are already walking through the door.

Not everyone welcomes the change. Critics argue that a library is for books, and that asking it to absorb work the state has stopped doing elsewhere leaves it doing many things adequately and none of them well. Librarians tend to answer that they did not choose the role; it arrived, in the form of people who had nowhere else to go, and turning them away was never a serious option.
